edges.description: Reduced nigrostriatal dopamine synthesis produces the childhood foot and limb dystonia that defines the DRD motor presentation.
The same central dopamine-synthesis deficit can present as focal dystonia, especially in the classic autosomal dominant subtype.
Progressive depletion of striatal dopamine in untreated childhood-onset DRD causes focal lower-limb dystonia to spread to the trunk and all four limbs as generalized dystonia.
Striatal dopamine deficiency in childhood-onset DRD characteristically drives acquired dystonic flexion-inversion (equinovarus posture) of the foot.
Dopamine deficiency in motor circuits explains parkinsonian features in older classic DRD and in severe TH-deficient and SPR-deficient disease.
Depletion of striatal dopamine impairs basal ganglia motor initiation and scaling, producing levodopa-responsive bradykinesia and hypokinesia.
Central dopamine depletion produces extrapyramidal cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity across DRD subtypes.
Dopamine deficiency in striato-thalamo-cortical and cerebellothalamic loops produces postural tremor in DRD.
Foot and limb dystonia from the dopamine-synthesis deficit produces the characteristic childhood gait disturbance.
Central dopamine deficiency in DRD frequently produces brisk deep tendon reflexes and pseudo-pyramidal signs that mimic cerebral palsy or spastic paraplegia.

Striatal dopamine deficiency across GCH1-, TH-, and SPR-deficient DRD produces appendicular dystonic and extrapyramidal limb hypertonia that frequently mimics spastic diplegia or hereditary spastic paraplegia.

Severe central dopamine depletion in autosomal recessive DRD (especially SPR and TH deficiency) causes paroxysmal dystonic conjugate upward deviation of the eyes (oculogyric crises) that responds to levodopa.
Early-infantile central dopamine deficiency impairs truncal postural tone, producing prominent axial hypotonia in recessive DRD subtypes.
Infantile-onset striatal dopamine deficiency in TH-deficient and SPR-deficient DRD impairs motor milestone acquisition, causing motor delay.
Homovanillic acid is the principal central dopamine metabolite, so impaired central dopamine synthesis directly lowers CSF homovanillic acid.
Limiting BH4 cofactor availability impairs tyrosine hydroxylation in nigrostriatal neurons and lowers downstream dopamine synthesis.
BH4 cofactor limitation can also impair phenylalanine hydroxylation, producing the transient hyperphenylalaninemia recorded for the GTPCH1-deficient branch.
intermediate_mechanisms: BH4 limitation impairs hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase cofactor support, producing transient or load-induced phenylalanine elevation.

edges.description: Reduced TH activity lowers catecholamine and dopamine synthesis, feeding the same central dopamine-deficiency endpoint as the BH4-limited branch.

nodes.description: GCH1-associated DRD (and rarer PTS and QDPR forms) reduces tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis or regeneration, limiting cofactor availability for tyrosine hydroxylase and other aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and feeding the shared `Striatal Dopamine Biosynthesis Impairment` endpoint. Heterozygous GCH1 variants cause partial BH4 deficiency that impairs nigrostriatal dopamine synthesis with only transient or phenylalanine-load-induced hyperphenylalaninemia, whereas biallelic GCH1, PTS, or QDPR variants cause more severe BH4 depletion accompanied by hyperphenylalaninemia.

nodes.description: In sepiapterin reductase-deficient DRD (DYT/PARK-SPR), biallelic pathogenic variants in SPR block the terminal step of de novo tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis and pterin salvage in the brain (where alternative aldo-keto/carbonyl reductases cannot compensate as they do in peripheral liver), leading to CSF accumulation of sepiapterin and dihydrobiopterin (BH2) and dual cofactor starvation of both tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase. nodes.description: The unifying mechanism across DRD subtypes is reduced dopamine biosynthesis in nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, arising either via tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor limitation (GCH1, SPR, PTS, QDPR) or via direct loss of tyrosine hydroxylase catalytic activity (TH). Because nigrostriatal dopaminergic terminals remain structurally intact, this functional neurotransmitter deficit produces diurnal childhood dystonia, pyramidal-like signs, and parkinsonism that respond dramatically and durably to exogenous levodopa.
